questions.q: In 2026 a company that has never used Snow devices must move 400 TB of video archives from a site with a weak, expensive network link. They want a physical transfer and must keep custody of their own drives at all times. What should they use?

options.t: Order a Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device
options.why: Wrong: Snowball Edge is no longer available to new customers, and AWS takes custody of the device once it is shipped back.

options.t: AWS DataSync over the existing link
options.why: Wrong: DataSync is the online option; over a weak, expensive link 400 TB would take too long and cost too much.

options.t: AWS Data Transfer Terminal
options.why: Right: you reserve a slot, bring your own storage devices to the terminal, upload over a very fast connection, and keep custody the whole time.

options.t: AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint
options.why: Wrong: it is for partners pushing files over SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2, still over the same weak network.

questions.explain: New customer + physical transfer + keep custody of own devices: Data Transfer Terminal.
questions.remember: Snowball Edge is closed to new customers. For new designs: online → DataSync, physical with your own devices → Data Transfer Terminal, edge compute → Outposts.
variants: The network is good and the transfer can finish in time → DataSync.
The question says a Snow device is already in use by an existing customer → Snow Family is still a valid answer.
The need is compute at a disconnected site, not transfer → Outposts.

questions.q: A team must copy 100 TB of files from its data center to S3 within one month. The site has a dedicated 1 Gbps link with spare capacity. Which approach is simplest?

options.t: AWS DataSync over the existing link
options.why: Right: 100 TB over 1 Gbps at about 80% efficiency takes roughly 11-12 days, well inside the deadline, with no shipping or device logistics.

options.t: An offline device job shipped to AWS
options.why: Wrong: offline transfer only wins when online transfer takes too long or costs too much; here it adds shipping and days to weeks of logistics.

options.t: AWS Database Migration Service
options.why: Wrong: DMS is for databases, not file transfers.

options.t: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN)
options.why: Wrong: MGN moves entire servers, not a file set into S3.

questions.explain: Do the network time math first: if the link finishes in time, use DataSync.
questions.remember: Time = data ÷ usable bandwidth. If online transfer fits the deadline and budget → DataSync; only when it takes too long or costs too much → offline (Snow if available, or Data Transfer Terminal).
variants: The same 100 TB over a 100 Mbps link (about 110 days) with a one-month deadline → offline method.
500 TB from a remote site with a 50 Mbps link → offline method, because online would take years.
Only a small one-time upload → S3 console or CLI.

questions.q: An existing Snow customer loaded the bulk of a file share onto devices and shipped them to AWS. Users keep changing files until the cutover weekend, several weeks later. How should the changes made after loading reach S3?

options.t: Order a second Snow job every week until cutover
options.why: Wrong: each job takes days to weeks end-to-end, so it can never keep up with ongoing changes.

options.t: The Snow device keeps replicating changes after it is shipped back
options.why: Wrong: a Snow job is a one-time offline copy; it has no change data capture.

options.t: Storage Gateway in front of the file share
options.why: Wrong: Storage Gateway gives local protocol access with a cache to S3; it is not the migration tool for syncing a delta before cutover.

options.t: Run AWS DataSync for the delta until cutover
options.why: Right: the standard pattern is Snow for the bulk first, then DataSync (or DMS CDC for databases) for the changes.

questions.explain: Snow is one-time; the delta goes online with DataSync or DMS.
questions.remember: Bulk first offline, delta online: Snow (or another offline method) for the bulk load, then DataSync for files or DMS CDC for databases until cutover.
variants: The source is a database that keeps changing → DMS with CDC after the bulk load.
There are no changes after the load → the offline job alone is enough.
The link is fast enough for the whole data set → DataSync from the start, no device needed.

questions.q: A security team will approve shipping regulated data on a Snowball Edge device only if a stolen device cannot reveal the encryption keys. Which statement about Snowball Edge answers their concern?

options.t: Data is encrypted only after AWS imports it into S3, using SSE-S3
options.why: Wrong: data is encrypted on the device itself, not only after import.

options.t: Data is encrypted on the device with 256-bit keys managed in AWS KMS, and the keys are not stored on the device
options.why: Right: the keys stay with KMS, so a lost or stolen device does not carry the keys needed to read the data.

options.t: The team must encrypt the files client-side because the device stores data in plain text
options.why: Wrong: the device encrypts data by default; extra client-side encryption is optional, not required.

options.t: The encryption key is printed on the E Ink shipping label so AWS can import the data
options.why: Wrong: the E Ink label shows the shipping address; keys are never shipped with the device.

questions.explain: Snow encryption uses KMS-managed 256-bit keys that never live on the device.
questions.remember: Snow device security: data encrypted on the device with KMS-managed 256-bit keys, keys not stored on the device. Use a KMS customer managed key for more control; losing KMS access blocks the import.
variants: The team wants to control and audit the key themselves → choose a KMS customer managed key for the job.
The question asks who may create jobs → IAM controls it, and CloudTrail logs the API calls.
The question asks how the job writes to the bucket → an IAM role on the job grants S3 access.

questions.q: A new design must run machine-learning inference on a research ship that has no internet connection for weeks. The company has no existing Snow devices. Which AWS option does AWS point new customers to for this edge compute need?

options.t: AWS DataSync
options.why: Wrong: DataSync is for online transfers; it does not run compute at a disconnected site.

options.t: AWS Data Transfer Terminal
options.why: Wrong: it is a physical site for uploading your own storage devices, not compute on board a ship.

options.t: AWS Outposts
options.why: Right: AWS points new customers to Outposts for edge computing, now that Snowball Edge is closed to new customers.

options.t: Snowball Edge Compute Optimized
options.why: Wrong: it is the legacy edge-compute answer, and Snowball Edge is no longer available to new customers.

questions.explain: Edge compute for a new customer: Outposts; Snowball Edge compute is legacy.
questions.remember: Edge compute → Outposts (current); Snowball Edge Compute Optimized only if the customer already uses Snow. Treat the Snow Family as legacy unless the question says a device is already in use.
variants: An existing Snow customer needs inference on the ship → Snowball Edge Compute Optimized is still possible.
The ship only needs to bring data back, not process it → Data Transfer Terminal or a partner solution.
The ship gets a good network link → DataSync for the transfer.
